lessons.subject: embryology
lessons.title: Congenital malformations: timing predicts the pattern
lessons.subtitle: Separate malformation, disruption, deformation, and the tests used to detect them

visual.caption: Teratogenic outcome depends most strongly on developmental timing, dose, and fetal susceptibility.

items.label: Weeks 0-2
items.detail: Severe injury usually causes embryonic death; surviving embryos often recover without a structural defect.

items.label: Weeks 3-8
items.detail: Organogenesis is the peak period for major structural malformations, with each organ having a specific critical window.

items.label: Week 9 to birth
items.detail: Growth, functional maturation, and the CNS remain vulnerable; major new structural defects are less common.

items.label: Screen
items.detail: Ultrasound and maternal serum or cell-free DNA estimate risk but do not by themselves establish every diagnosis.

items.label: Diagnose
items.detail: CVS samples placental tissue earlier; amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid later for definitive fetal testing when indicated.

essentials: A malformation is an intrinsic developmental error; a disruption destroys previously normal tissue; a deformation results from mechanical force.
The embryonic period, especially weeks 3-8, is the most sensitive window for major structural malformations.
Risk depends on dose, duration, timing, maternal-fetal genotype, and simultaneous exposures.
Folate before conception and early pregnancy reduces neural-tube-defect risk.
A screening test changes probability; a diagnostic test establishes or excludes a condition with far greater certainty.

traps.wrong: Every teratogenic exposure causes the same defect throughout pregnancy.
traps.right: The same exposure can cause death, malformation, growth restriction, or functional injury depending on timing and dose.

traps.wrong: A positive screening result is a confirmed fetal diagnosis.
traps.right: Screening identifies increased risk and generally requires diagnostic confirmation.

recognition: A major structural defect following exposure during organogenesis points to a teratogenic malformation.
Abnormal positioning caused by uterine constraint is a deformation rather than a primary malformation.
CVS is the earlier invasive sampling option; amniocentesis is performed later.

source.label: Langman's Medical Embryology, 15th ed.
source.detail: Birth defects, teratology, and prenatal diagnosis chapter; confirmed TUMS curriculum.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Chemical synaptic transmission from impulse to response
lessons.subtitle: Release, receptor action, postsynaptic potentials, and signal termination

visual.caption: Chemical transmission is unidirectional because release machinery is presynaptic and receptors are postsynaptic.

items.label: Arrival
items.detail: A presynaptic action potential depolarizes the terminal and opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.

items.label: Release
items.detail: Ca2+ binds the vesicle-fusion machinery, causing SNARE-dependent exocytosis of transmitter quanta.

items.label: Receptor
items.detail: Ionotropic receptors directly gate channels; metabotropic receptors act through G proteins and second messengers.

items.label: Integration
items.detail: EPSPs bring membrane voltage toward threshold; IPSPs oppose firing by hyperpolarization or shunting.

items.label: Termination
items.detail: Transmitter is removed by enzymatic degradation, reuptake into neuron or glia, or diffusion away.

essentials: Postsynaptic potentials are graded and can summate temporally and spatially; action potentials are all-or-none.
An EPSP or IPSP is defined by its effect on firing probability, not by one universally fixed ion.
Small-molecule transmitters are commonly synthesized in terminals and stored in small clear vesicles; neuropeptides are synthesized in the soma.
Acetylcholine is terminated mainly by acetylcholinesterase; monoamines and many amino-acid transmitters rely heavily on reuptake.
Presynaptic inhibition often reduces Ca2+ entry and therefore reduces transmitter release.

traps.wrong: Ca2+ carries the propagated nerve action potential down the axon.
traps.right: Na+ and K+ dominate the axonal spike; terminal Ca2+ entry triggers vesicle release.

traps.wrong: Every inhibitory synapse simply makes the membrane more negative.
traps.right: Inhibition may hyperpolarize or shunt excitatory current by increasing membrane conductance.

recognition: A delay between presynaptic depolarization and postsynaptic response indicates a chemical synapse.
A receptor producing a rapid millisecond current is usually ionotropic; a slower amplified response is usually metabotropic.
Reduced quantal release after blocking terminal Ca2+ channels localizes the defect presynaptically.

source.label: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 2026
source.detail: Synaptic transmission and neurotransmitter sections; confirmed TUMS Tissue, Development & Function curriculum.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Hemoglobin turns structure into cooperative oxygen delivery
lessons.subtitle: Heme chemistry, T-R transition, 2,3-BPG, Bohr effect, CO, and methemoglobin

visual.caption: O2 binding shifts hemoglobin from the low-affinity T state toward the high-affinity R state.

items.label: Heme
items.detail: Each globin chain holds one protoporphyrin IX with Fe2+, which binds one O2 molecule reversibly.

items.label: T state
items.detail: Deoxyhemoglobin has lower O2 affinity and a larger central cavity that binds 2,3-BPG.

items.label: R state
items.detail: O2 binding changes heme and globin conformation, increasing the affinity of remaining subunits.

items.label: Right shift
items.detail: Higher H+, CO2, temperature, or 2,3-BPG lowers affinity and promotes tissue unloading.

items.label: Abnormal ligands
items.detail: CO binds Fe2+ with high affinity and left-shifts remaining sites; Fe3+ methemoglobin cannot bind O2.

essentials: Adult HbA is α2β2; fetal HbF is α2γ2 and binds 2,3-BPG less strongly, giving it higher oxygen affinity.
Hemoglobin has a sigmoidal O2 curve because subunits cooperate; monomeric myoglobin has a hyperbolic curve.
The Bohr effect is reduced O2 affinity at higher H+ and CO2, aiding oxygen unloading in metabolically active tissue.
2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the T state.
Oxidation of heme iron from Fe2+ to Fe3+ produces methemoglobin, which does not bind oxygen normally.

traps.wrong: Oxygen binds directly to ferric Fe3+ in normal hemoglobin.
traps.right: Normal oxygen binding requires ferrous Fe2+; Fe3+ defines methemoglobin.

traps.wrong: A right shift means hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly.
traps.right: A right shift means lower affinity and easier tissue unloading.

recognition: A sigmoidal saturation curve identifies cooperative hemoglobin rather than myoglobin.
Low P50 means high oxygen affinity; high P50 means reduced affinity.
Normal PaO2 with impaired oxygen content after CO exposure reflects dysfunctional hemoglobin binding.

source.label: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry
source.detail: Chapter 3, globular hemeproteins; confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules curriculum.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Carbohydrate structure: classify first, then predict reactivity
lessons.subtitle: Aldose versus ketose, stereochemistry, anomers, bonds, and reducing sugars

visual.caption: The free anomeric carbon determines whether a sugar can open into a reducing form.

items.label: Monosaccharides
items.detail: Glucose and galactose are aldohexoses; fructose is a ketohexose. Ring closure creates an α or β anomer.

items.label: Epimers
items.detail: Glucose and galactose differ at C4; glucose and mannose differ at C2.

items.label: Maltose
items.detail: Glucose-α(1→4)-glucose; one anomeric carbon remains free, so maltose is reducing.

items.label: Lactose
items.detail: Galactose-β(1→4)-glucose; the glucose anomeric carbon remains free, so lactose is reducing.

items.label: Sucrose
items.detail: Glucose-α1↔β2-fructose joins both anomeric carbons and is therefore nonreducing.

essentials: D/L configuration is defined relative to glyceraldehyde and is not the same as the direction of optical rotation.
Anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon; epimers differ at one other stereocenter.
Mutarotation is interconversion of α and β anomers through the open-chain form.
A reducing sugar needs a free anomeric carbon capable of forming an open-chain carbonyl.
Lactase hydrolyzes lactose; sucrase hydrolyzes sucrose; maltase hydrolyzes maltose.

traps.wrong: Every disaccharide is nonreducing.
traps.right: Maltose and lactose are reducing; sucrose is nonreducing because both anomeric carbons form the bond.

traps.wrong: Glucose and fructose are epimers.
traps.right: They are constitutional isomers: glucose is an aldose and fructose is a ketose.

recognition: A ring carbon bonded to two oxygens is the anomeric carbon.
A glycosidic bond involving both anomeric carbons identifies a nonreducing disaccharide.
Rapid Seliwanoff positivity supports a ketose such as fructose.

source.label: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry
source.detail: Chapter 7, carbohydrate structure; confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules curriculum.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Glycoconjugates organize recognition, membranes, and extracellular matrix
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish glycoproteins, proteoglycans, glycolipids, and GPI anchors

visual.caption: Classify a glycoconjugate by its backbone, carbohydrate proportion, and cellular location.

items.label: Glycoprotein
items.detail: A protein bearing relatively short, branched oligosaccharides; common in receptors, antibodies, enzymes, and adhesion molecules.

items.label: Proteoglycan
items.detail: A core protein bearing long, unbranched sulfated GAG chains; highly hydrated and abundant in extracellular matrix.

items.label: Glycolipid
items.detail: A membrane lipid with an extracellular carbohydrate head; important in recognition and blood-group antigens.

items.label: N-linked
items.detail: Oligosaccharide attaches to asparagine and is initiated in the rough ER before Golgi processing.

items.label: O-linked and GPI
items.detail: O-linked sugars attach mainly to serine/threonine in Golgi; GPI anchors tether proteins to the outer membrane leaflet.

essentials: GAGs are repeating disaccharides, usually highly negatively charged and water-binding.
Proteoglycans resist compression and regulate diffusion/signaling in extracellular matrix.
N-linked oligosaccharides attach to asparagine; O-linked chains attach mainly to serine or threonine.
Cell-surface carbohydrates face the extracellular space and contribute to the glycocalyx.
ABO antigens are terminal carbohydrate structures on glycoproteins and glycolipids.

traps.wrong: Proteoglycans are mostly protein with a few short branched sugars.
traps.right: That better describes glycoproteins; proteoglycans are dominated by long GAG chains.

traps.wrong: Membrane carbohydrate chains normally face the cytosol.
traps.right: They face the noncytosolic/extracellular side of the membrane.

recognition: A bottle-brush ECM molecule with many long charged chains is a proteoglycan.
A membrane recognition determinant attached to ceramide is a glycolipid.
A carbohydrate attached to asparagine is N-linked.

source.label: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry
source.detail: Carbohydrate and complex-carbohydrate sections; confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules curriculum.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: DNA repair: match the lesion to the repair pathway
lessons.subtitle: Mismatch repair, BER, NER, homologous recombination, and end joining

visual.caption: Identify the lesion first; the correct pathway follows from what must be removed or rebuilt.

items.label: Mismatch repair
items.detail: Corrects replication mismatches and short insertion-deletion loops missed by proofreading.

items.label: Base-excision repair
items.detail: A DNA glycosylase removes one damaged base; AP endonuclease, polymerase, and ligase restore the site.

items.label: Nucleotide-excision repair
items.detail: A short oligonucleotide containing a bulky helix-distorting lesion is excised and resynthesized.

items.label: Homologous recombination
items.detail: Repairs double-strand breaks accurately by copying a homologous template, mainly in S/G2.

items.label: Nonhomologous end joining
items.detail: Directly rejoins broken ends without a homologous template and can lose or add nucleotides.

essentials: Polymerase proofreading occurs during synthesis; mismatch repair corrects errors that escape proofreading.
BER removes an individual abnormal base, whereas NER removes a short stretch around a bulky lesion.
Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide-excision repair of UV-induced damage.
Lynch syndrome results from inherited mismatch-repair defects and microsatellite instability.
BRCA pathway defects impair homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks.

traps.wrong: UV thymine dimers are normally fixed by mismatch repair.
traps.right: Bulky UV photoproducts are removed by nucleotide-excision repair.

traps.wrong: Nonhomologous end joining requires a sister chromatid template.
traps.right: NHEJ directly joins ends without a homologous template; homologous recombination uses the template.

recognition: Extreme UV sensitivity and skin-cancer risk indicate defective NER.
Microsatellite instability indicates defective mismatch repair.
Repair using the sister chromatid after replication indicates homologous recombination.

source.label: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry
source.detail: DNA replication and repair section; confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules curriculum.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.topic: Practical amino acid and protein tests
lessons.title: Amino-acid and protein tests by reaction target
lessons.subtitle: Use the detected chemical group and positive color to identify the assay
topicPatterns: Practical amino acid and protein tests

visual.caption: The most reliable memory anchor is the chemical target, followed by the positive appearance.

items.label: Ninhydrin
items.detail: Most free α-amino groups produce blue-purple Ruhemann's purple; imino acids such as proline give yellow.

items.label: Biuret
items.detail: Cu2+ complexes with multiple peptide bonds in alkaline solution to produce violet color.

items.label: Xanthoproteic
items.detail: Nitration of aromatic residues gives yellow that deepens to orange in alkali.

items.label: Millon
items.detail: The phenolic group of tyrosine produces a red reaction product.

items.label: Sulfur test
items.detail: Sulfur released from cysteine/cystine can form a dark lead-sulfide precipitate.

essentials: Biuret requires multiple peptide bonds and is therefore a protein/peptide test rather than a sensitive free-amino-acid test.
Ninhydrin is broadly useful for amino acids and for visualizing separated amino acids on chromatography media.
Proline gives a yellow ninhydrin product because its amino group is secondary.
A blank controls for color contributed by reagents and solvent rather than analyte.
Positive color intensity is not automatically quantitative unless the method is calibrated.

traps.wrong: Biuret detects the biuret molecule specifically in protein samples.
traps.right: The named reaction detects coordinated peptide bonds in proteins and sufficiently long peptides.

traps.wrong: Every amino acid gives the same purple ninhydrin color.
traps.right: Proline and hydroxyproline characteristically give yellow products.

recognition: Violet alkaline copper reaction indicates Biuret.
Purple spots after spraying a chromatogram indicate ninhydrin-positive amino acids.
Yellow-to-orange reaction after nitric acid suggests aromatic residues.

source.label: Confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules practical curriculum
source.detail: Amino-acid practical block; standard qualitative biochemistry laboratory reactions.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Enzyme assays: measure initial rate, not just final color
lessons.subtitle: Controls, temperature, pH, substrate concentration, and activity calculations

visual.caption: A valid assay converts a calibrated signal change into product formed per unit time.

items.label: Prepare controls
items.detail: Use a reagent blank and a negative control lacking active enzyme or substrate.

items.label: Control conditions
items.detail: Keep pH, temperature, ionic strength, volumes, and incubation timing constant.

items.label: Start reaction
items.detail: Add the initiating component consistently, mix, and begin timing immediately.

items.label: Measure initial rate
items.detail: Use the early linear change before substrate depletion, product inhibition, or enzyme instability distorts velocity.

items.label: Report activity
items.detail: Convert signal through a standard curve or extinction coefficient and report amount converted per time.

essentials: One enzyme unit commonly represents 1 µmol of substrate converted per minute under stated conditions.
Boiling usually reduces measured activity by denaturing the enzyme without removing substrate.
Initial velocity is proportional to enzyme concentration when substrate is abundant and conditions are fixed.
A pH or temperature optimum is assay-specific and reflects both catalysis and protein stability.
A standard curve is required when instrument response cannot be converted directly from a known extinction coefficient.

traps.wrong: The darkest final tube always had the greatest initial velocity.
traps.right: Final color also depends on incubation time, substrate depletion, and linearity; compare controlled initial slopes.

traps.wrong: A blank without analyte is unnecessary if the solution looks colorless.
traps.right: Reagents and cuvette can absorb light even when no visible color is obvious.

recognition: A straight early absorbance-versus-time segment is the interval used for initial velocity.
Loss of activity after boiling supports an enzyme-dependent reaction.
Doubling enzyme concentration should approximately double initial rate when substrate is not limiting.

source.label: Confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules practical curriculum
source.detail: Enzyme practical block; Lippincott enzyme kinetics principles.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Spectrophotometry: blank, wavelength, absorbance, concentration
lessons.subtitle: Use Beer-Lambert correctly and recognize when the reading is unreliable

visual.caption: A spectrophotometer compares incident with transmitted light at a selected wavelength.

items.label: Select λ
items.detail: Measure near the analyte's λmax for greatest sensitivity and reproducibility.

items.label: Blank
items.detail: Zero the instrument with solvent and all reagents except analyte.

items.label: Measure
items.detail: The detector measures transmitted light; absorbance A = -log10(T).

items.label: Calculate
items.detail: Within the linear range, A = εlc, so absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Dilute samples above the linear range and reject dirty, scratched, bubbled, or mismatched cuvettes.

essentials: Absorbance is logarithmically related to transmittance and is directly proportional to concentration only within the linear range.
The blank contains every non-analyte component used in the sample.
Cuvette orientation and path length must remain consistent between standards and unknowns.
A calibration curve plots known concentration against measured response and is used to interpolate an unknown.
Turbidity scatters light and can falsely increase apparent absorbance.

traps.wrong: Double concentration always doubles percent transmittance.
traps.right: Within the linear range, concentration is proportional to absorbance, not percent transmittance.

traps.wrong: The blank should contain the analyte at the same concentration as the sample.
traps.right: The blank contains solvent and reagents but omits the analyte being measured.

recognition: A plot of absorbance versus concentration should be linear over the validated working range.
An unexpectedly high reading with visible bubbles suggests optical interference.
A = 0 corresponds to 100% transmittance.

source.label: Confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules practical curriculum
source.detail: Spectrophotometer block; standard Beer-Lambert laboratory principles.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: DNA extraction: release, protect, separate, precipitate
lessons.subtitle: Know why detergent, salt, protease, and alcohol are used

visual.caption: Each reagent removes one barrier between intact cells and visible purified DNA.

items.label: Lyse
items.detail: Detergent disrupts lipid cell and nuclear membranes, releasing nucleic acids and proteins.

items.label: Protect
items.detail: Cold conditions and chelation of divalent cations reduce nuclease activity.

items.label: Remove protein
items.detail: Protease digests histones and enzymes; salt helps dissociate and aggregate contaminants.

items.label: Precipitate
items.detail: Salt neutralizes phosphate charge and cold ethanol or isopropanol lowers DNA solubility.

items.label: Recover
items.detail: Spool or pellet the DNA, wash with alcohol, dry briefly, and redissolve in suitable buffer.

essentials: Detergent lyses membranes; it does not specifically cut DNA into fragments.
EDTA protects DNA by chelating Mg2+ and other divalent cofactors required by many nucleases.
DNA precipitates poorly from alcohol without sufficient cations to shield its negatively charged phosphate backbone.
Vigorous mixing after high-molecular-weight DNA is released can shear it mechanically.
The A260/A280 ratio is commonly used as a rough purity check for nucleic acid versus protein contamination.

traps.wrong: Cold ethanol dissolves DNA so it disappears into solution.
traps.right: Alcohol lowers DNA solubility and causes DNA to precipitate.

traps.wrong: Protease is added to hydrolyze the DNA backbone.
traps.right: Protease removes histones and contaminating enzymes while preserving DNA.

recognition: White stringy material at the alcohol interface is precipitated high-molecular-weight DNA.
A low A260/A280 ratio suggests protein contamination.
Highly fragmented DNA after harsh vortexing suggests mechanical shearing.

source.label: Confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules practical curriculum
source.detail: DNA extraction block; standard nucleic-acid purification principles.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Chromatography separates by unequal partitioning
lessons.subtitle: Stationary phase, mobile phase, Rf, charge, size, and affinity

visual.caption: A component moves faster when it prefers the mobile phase and slower when it interacts strongly with the stationary phase.

items.label: Paper/TLC
items.detail: Components separate by differential partition or adsorption; Rf = distance solute / distance solvent front.

items.label: Ion exchange
items.detail: A charged matrix binds oppositely charged molecules, which are eluted by changing salt or pH.

items.label: Size exclusion
items.detail: Large molecules bypass bead pores and elute before smaller molecules that enter the pores.

items.label: Affinity
items.detail: A specific immobilized ligand captures the target, which is later released by competition or altered conditions.

items.label: Read the plate
items.detail: Mark the origin and solvent front immediately; visualize separated spots without letting the solvent cover the sample origin.

essentials: The mobile phase moves; the stationary phase remains fixed.
Rf is unitless and is only comparable when stationary phase, solvent, temperature, and other conditions match.
A compound with stronger stationary-phase interaction generally migrates less in planar chromatography.
In size-exclusion chromatography, large molecules elute first because they sample less internal bead volume.
Affinity chromatography offers high selectivity through a specific ligand-target interaction.

traps.wrong: The solvent front distance is divided by the solute distance to calculate Rf.
traps.right: Rf = distance traveled by solute divided by distance traveled by solvent front.

traps.wrong: Small molecules always elute first in size-exclusion chromatography.
traps.right: Large molecules are excluded from pores and therefore elute first.

recognition: A spot halfway to the solvent front has an Rf of approximately 0.5.
A column using an antibody to isolate one antigen is affinity chromatography.
A salt gradient releasing bound proteins suggests ion-exchange chromatography.

source.label: Confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules practical curriculum
source.detail: Chromatography block; standard biochemical separation principles.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Flame photometry converts atomic emission into ion concentration
lessons.subtitle: Nebulization, excitation, wavelength selection, calibration, and interference

visual.caption: The instrument measures element-specific light emitted as flame-excited atoms return to lower energy levels.

items.label: Nebulize
items.detail: The liquid sample is converted into a fine aerosol and carried into the flame.

items.label: Atomize
items.detail: Solvent evaporates and salts dissociate to produce free atoms.

items.label: Excite
items.detail: Thermal energy raises electrons to excited states.

items.label: Emit
items.detail: Atoms emit characteristic wavelengths as electrons return to lower energy levels.

items.label: Quantify
items.detail: A wavelength filter and detector measure intensity, which is compared with standards in the valid range.

essentials: Flame photometry is especially useful for alkali metals such as sodium, potassium, and lithium.
It is an emission method: the instrument measures light produced by excited atoms, not light absorbed by molecules.
A reagent blank sets background and a calibration curve relates emission intensity to concentration.
Samples and standards should have similar matrix composition to reduce viscosity and ionization effects.
Readings outside the calibration range require dilution and correction by the dilution factor.

traps.wrong: Flame photometry primarily measures peptide-bond absorbance.
traps.right: It measures characteristic atomic emission, commonly from Na+, K+, or Li+.

traps.wrong: Unknown concentration can be read reliably beyond the highest standard.
traps.right: Dilute the unknown into the validated calibration range.

recognition: A nebulizer feeding a flame followed by an optical filter identifies a flame photometer.
Characteristic emission intensity increasing with sodium standards forms the calibration curve.
An unknown above the top standard should be diluted before quantification.

source.label: Confirmed TUMS Cell & Molecules practical curriculum
source.detail: Flame-photometry block; standard clinical chemistry principles.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Osmosis practical: predict water movement from effective osmoles
lessons.subtitle: Separate osmolarity, tonicity, permeability, and final cell volume

visual.caption: Water moves toward the side with greater effective concentration of nonpenetrating solute.

items.label: Hypotonic outside
items.detail: Water enters cells; animal cells swell and may lyse.

items.label: Isotonic outside
items.detail: Effective osmotic forces balance and cell volume remains stable.

items.label: Hypertonic outside
items.detail: Water leaves cells, causing shrinkage or RBC crenation.

items.label: Penetrating solute
items.detail: A solution may be isosmotic initially yet hypotonic after the solute enters and water follows.

items.label: Dialysis setup
items.detail: Small permeant solutes cross the membrane; retained macromolecules create sustained osmotic effects.

essentials: Osmolarity counts all dissolved particles; tonicity predicts final cell volume from effective nonpenetrating solutes.
Water crosses toward higher effective osmotic pressure until balanced by opposing forces.
RBC hemolysis indicates excessive water entry; crenation indicates water loss.
Urea can make a solution initially isosmotic but is ineffective for sustained tonicity because it penetrates many cell membranes.
Mass change of a dialysis bag reflects net water movement plus any permeant-solute movement.

traps.wrong: Isosmotic and isotonic always mean the same thing.
traps.right: A penetrating solute contributes to measured osmolarity but not sustained tonicity.

traps.wrong: Water moves toward the lower solute concentration.
traps.right: Across a water-permeable membrane, water moves toward the side with more effective nonpenetrating solute.

recognition: Swollen or lysed RBCs indicate a hypotonic external solution.
Crenated RBCs indicate a hypertonic external solution.
A dialysis bag gaining mass contains the greater effective concentration of retained solute.

source.label: Guyton and Hall + confirmed TUMS practical curriculum
source.detail: Membrane transport and osmosis principles applied to the Cell & Molecules practical.
